lead: Bias a transistor at a fixed Q-point, add a signal of a few millivolts, and over that small swing the device behaves as a linear two-port. Three equivalent pictures describe it. The h-parameter model is what you measure in the lab, the hybrid-π model is what device physics gives you, and the T-model puts the resistance in the emitter where the emitter follower and common-base stage are easiest to read. Every gain, input resistance and output resistance in this unit comes from one of these three, and you convert between them with simple arithmetic.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the Q-point and Chapter 2.2 for the DC currents that fix g_m, r_π and r_e.

sections.h3: The same device as a two-port

blocks.text: Bias the transistor and the currents settle at a Q-point. Add a signal of a few millivolts on top and, over that small swing, the curves are straight lines. The transistor is now a linear two-port: a base-emitter input port and a collector-emitter output port. All three models in this chapter describe that one two-port, and any one converts into the others.
v_be = h_ie·i_b + h_re·v_ce      i_c = h_fe·i_b + h_oe·v_ce
blocks.where: v_be and i_b are the signal voltage and current at the input port; v_ce and i_c are the same at the output port. Lowercase letters mean small-signal changes around the Q-point, never DC totals.

items: h_ie — input resistance measured with the output shorted (v_ce = 0), in ohms.
h_fe — forward current gain measured with the output shorted; this is the β of the datasheet.
h_re — reverse voltage feedback measured with the input open (i_b = 0); a small number, about 10⁻⁴.
h_oe — output admittance measured with the input open, in siemens; it equals 1/r_o.

blocks.text: The name hybrid is honest: the four numbers carry mixed units, ohms, a pure ratio, a pure ratio, siemens. The subscript tells you the test: the first letter is the common terminal (e for emitter), the second is the quantity (i input, f forward, r reverse, o output).

The full box needs a feedback voltage source h_re v_ce in the input loop and a current source h_fe i_b at the output. Hand analysis uses the CE approximate model instead: h_re is about 10⁻⁴ so it is dropped, and h_oe is dropped when R_L is far below r_o. What remains is h_ie in series with the base and one current source h_fe i_b at the collector.
The hybrid-π model is built from device physics, so its elements follow the bias current instead of being re-measured at every Q-point. Some syllabi call it the Giacoletto model.

blocks.where: g_m is the transconductance in siemens; I_C is the DC collector current at the Q-point in amperes; V_T = kT/q where k is the Boltzmann constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K), T is the absolute temperature in kelvin and q is the electron charge (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C); at T ≈ 300 K, V_T ≈ 26 mV.

blocks.text: r_π = β / g_m = β V_T / I_C
blocks.where: r_π is the base-emitter resistance of the model in ohms; β is the DC current gain; g_m and I_C are as above.
r_o is the output resistance in ohms; V_A is the Early voltage, typically 50 V to 150 V; I_C is in amperes.

blocks.text: At I_C = 1 mA and V_T = 26 mV, g_m = 38.5 mS. Every milliamp of collector current buys roughly 38.5 mS, so g_m is fixed by bias alone and β never enters it.

Three more elements sit in the full model. r_x is the base spreading resistance between the base terminal and the active region under the emitter, roughly 10 Ω to 300 Ω. C_π and C_µ are capacitances that do nothing at low frequency and take over at high frequency (see Unit 3, Frequency Response and Power Amplifiers).

The controlled source is g_m v_be, and v_be is the voltage across r_π. Once r_x is present, the base terminal voltage is not v_be; that difference matters only when the source resistance is very small. Exams normally set r_x = 0.

The T-model puts the resistance in the emitter leg. It is the natural picture for the emitter follower and the common-base stage (Chapter 2.5), and for any stage where the emitter is not at signal ground.

blocks.where: r_e is the emitter resistance in ohms; α = β/(β+1) is the common-base current gain, just under 1; I_E is the DC emitter current, (β+1)I_B, nearly equal to I_C.

blocks.text: The source in the T-model is α i_e. With I_C = 1 mA, r_e = 0.99/38.5 mS = 26 Ω, the familiar number r_e ≈ 26 mV / I_E. The two models agree because the base and emitter resistances are the same resistance seen from different terminals:

blocks.where: r_π is the hybrid-π input resistance in ohms; β is the DC current gain; r_e is the T-model emitter resistance in ohms. Check: 101 × 26 Ω = 2.6 kΩ.

Model symbol
Value at I_C = 1 mA, β = 100, V_A = 100 V

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach the full T-model with r_x. When it is included, r_x sits in series with the base and nothing else in the model changes.

figure.caption: All three boxes describe the same transistor at the same operating point; only the numbers you are handed change. The example converts the 1 mA, β = 100 device across all three.

spec.title: One device, three models
spec.aria: Four boxes left to right: the biased transistor at 1 mA, its h-parameter two-port, the hybrid-pi model and the T-model, joined by measured and convert arrows.

examples.question: An npn transistor is biased at I_C = 1 mA with β = 100 and Early voltage V_A = 100 V. Take V_T = 26 mV. (a) Find g_m, r_π and r_o. (b) With R_L = 5 kΩ and r_o included, find the stage voltage gain A_v = −g_m(R_L ∥ r_o). (c) Write the h-parameters and the T-model value for the same device.
steps: r_o = V_A / I_C = 100 V / 1 mA = 100 kΩ.
Stage voltage gain A_v = −g_m (R_L ∥ r_o) = −38.46 mS × 4.762 kΩ = −183.2. The minus sign says the CE stage inverts.
h-parameters: h_fe = β = 100, h_ie = r_π = 2.6 kΩ, h_oe = 1/r_o = 1/100 kΩ = 10 µS, h_re is of order 10⁻⁴ and is neglected.
T-model: α = β/(β+1) = 100/101 = 0.990, so r_e = α/g_m = 0.990/38.46 mS = 25.7 Ω, which rounds to 26 mV/I_E = 26 Ω.
examples.answer: g_m = 38.46 mS, r_π = 2.6 kΩ, r_o = 100 kΩ, stage voltage gain A_v = −183.2 with R_L = 5 kΩ, and h_ie = 2.6 kΩ, h_fe = 100, h_oe = 10 µS, r_e = 26 Ω.
examples.check:
gm = 1e-3/26e-3
rpi = 100/gm
ro = 100/1e-3
rp = 5e3*ro/(5e3+ro)
av = -gm*rp
print(round(gm*1000, 2))
print(round(rpi, 1))
print(round(ro, 1))
print(round(rp, 1))
print(round(av, 2))

traps: Mixing the models: quoting h_ie from a datasheet at one bias current and r_π from a different I_C, then using both in the same calculation.
Dropping the minus sign. The common-emitter stage inverts, so A_v = −g_m(R_L ∥ r_o); a positive answer means you lost it.
Using R_L alone when r_o is given. The gain formula needs R_L ∥ r_o, and the two differ by 5 % here, more when R_L is close to r_o.
Confusing α with β, and r_e with r_π. The bridge is r_π = (β + 1) r_e, not r_π = β r_e.

Treating 26 mV as a constant. V_T = kT/q rises with temperature, so g_m falls and r_e rises unless the bias current is raised in proportion to V_T (a PTAT bias). With I_C ∝ V_T, g_m = I_C/V_T and r_e = V_T/I_E stay fixed.

quiz.q: Define h_fe and state the condition under which it is measured.
quiz.a: h_fe is the forward current gain, i_c/i_b with the output shorted (v_ce = 0). It equals the DC β of the transistor.

quiz.q: Write g_m in terms of I_C and give V_T at room temperature.
quiz.a: g_m = I_C/V_T; V_T = kT/q ≈ 26 mV near 300 K.

quiz.q: Why is h_re dropped in the CE approximate model?
quiz.a: h_re is about 10⁻⁴, so the feedback term h_re v_ce is a fraction of a millivolt even for volts at the collector. Its effect on the input is well under one per cent, smaller than the spread in β.

quiz.q: A transistor has I_C = 2 mA, β = 150, V_A = 80 V and V_T = 26 mV. Find g_m, r_π and r_o.
An emitter follower runs at I_E = 0.5 mA. Find r_e and r_π for β = 120.
A student reports r_π = 2.6 kΩ and h_ie = 5 kΩ for the same transistor in the same circuit. What has gone wrong?
quiz.a: h_ie and r_π are the same quantity in the two models, so they must be equal at a given Q-point. Two values mean two bias currents, usually a datasheet h_ie taken at a different I_C than the circuit's.

quiz.q: The hybrid-π model always shows r_o, yet the CE approximate h-model often drops h_oe. Are these consistent?
quiz.a: Yes. h_oe = 1/r_o, the same element. It is dropped only when R_L ≪ r_o, where it changes the gain by a few per cent. When R_L is comparable to r_o the parallel combination visibly lowers gain, so r_o is kept.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production design uses the Gummel-Poon model in SPICE, and CMOS design uses BSIM, which carries hundreds of parameters but still keeps g_m, r_o and the junction capacitances of this chapter at its core. Pulling those numbers out of measured S-parameters is a recognised job in RF and analog IC groups. Search 'Gummel-Poon model', 'BSIM4' and 'small-signal extraction from S-parameters' to go further.
